standfirst: A two-week catch-up issue to open the run. Jane Schoenbrun turns the slasher inside out for MUBI, Eric Goode finds another American subculture to sit inside, Netflix closes its Manson file, and Locarno is mid-festival on the lake while Venice, Telluride, Toronto and New York have all shown their hands.
coverNote: Picks are marked with a dot. Director, cinematographer and scores are reserved for picks; everything else runs one line. Scores were checked when this issue was compiled — *not yet rated* means no published score was available at that point. A bordered tag flags work dealing in cults, conspiracy movements or political extremism.

sections.title: Television
sections.kicker: Fifteen days of premieres across HBO, Netflix, Apple TV+, Prime Video, Hulu and the BBC. Three of them are worth your evening; the rest are here so you can see what you are skipping.

blocks.text: An unusually strong fortnight for non-fiction. The best thing on television right now is a five-part series about lizards, which is not a sentence anyone expected to write, and the week's most quietly alarming hour is a BBC documentary about men who want to build their own countries.

blocks.title: Monsters of God
blocks.meta: HBO / HBO Max · five parts · premiered August 6
why: Goode made *Tiger King*, and the temptation is to file this next to it and move on. Don't. Where that series ran on chaos, this one runs on patience — years of embedded access to reptile traffickers, collectors and the federal agents chasing them, with Goode's camera holding on people long after a normal documentary would cut away.

The reptiles are the pretext. The subject is the particular American appetite for owning something rare enough to justify a life built around it, and Goode films that appetite with the deadpan curiosity Errol Morris brings to his own obsessives. It took the Audience Award in SXSW's TV Premieres section in March and arrives without a bad review on the board.

blocks.title: The Bombing of Pan Am 103
blocks.extraCredit: Created by Jonathan Lee & Adam Morane-Griffiths
why: A BBC co-production that ran in the UK first and has now landed in the US, where it went to No. 2 worldwide inside a week. Lee's second pass at the Lockerbie material strips out every sensational instinct the subject invites and stays with the procedure: Scottish local police and the FBI, thrown together in a field of wreckage, working a case that took twelve years to reach a courtroom.

The restraint is the point and also the limit — the Hollywood Reporter's line, that it delivers a less-than-memorable portrait of an indelible event, is fair. But the reconstruction of how the investigation actually held together is superb, and the show never once reaches for the bomber's psychology as entertainment.

blocks.title: Conversations with a Killer: The Charles Manson Tapes
blocks.extraCredit: Fifth and final season of the series
why: Netflix retires the format on its most over-covered subject, which makes the framing the whole question: this one goes at Manson as a recruiter rather than a murderer — how the Family was assembled, what it offered the people who joined, and how a trial became a national performance.

Worth a look if *Wild Wild Country* is the register you want — the machinery of belief rather than the body count. It is three episodes, it arrived yesterday, and no critical consensus has formed yet.

sections.title: In Cinemas
sections.kicker: Two of the best-reviewed American films of the year opened in the space of a week, and one of them is a summer-camp slasher. The multiplex, meanwhile, belongs entirely to one film.

blocks.text: Spider-Man ran away with both weekends and will finish the year as the biggest film in the world, which is the least interesting thing that happened in cinemas this fortnight. The interesting thing is that MUBI put a 35mm slasher into theatres and it came out at a hundred per cent.

blocks.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma
blocks.meta: MUBI · limited, August 7 · world premiere at Cannes, May 13
why: Schoenbrun's third feature and their best-reviewed by a distance — not a slasher pastiche but a film about what the slasher did to the people who grew up inside it, with Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson anchoring a story that keeps folding back into itself. Variety's Jessica Kiang called it their most accomplished, most persuasive and most playful work, which is the right order of adjectives.

Eric Yue's second outing with Schoenbrun after *I Saw the TV Glow*, again on 35mm, and the grain is doing real argumentative work here rather than decorating the thing. If you want formally distinctive genre filmmaking with a directorial signature you could pick out of a lineup, this is the film of the fortnight and it is not close.

blocks.title: I Want Your Sex
blocks.meta: Magnolia Pictures · limited, July 31 · Sundance 2026 premiere · US VOD September 1
why: Araki's first feature in a decade, and the reviews and the audience have landed in completely different places — certified fresh at ninety per cent, sitting at 5.6 with users. That gap is the most Araki thing about it.

Korte's candy-coloured photography builds the cartoon world Araki has always needed, so that the real feeling can arrive sideways. Olivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman carry an erotic comedy that is funnier and more provocative than it is deep, which is a fair trade for having him back at all.

blocks.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma

sections.title: Streaming
sections.kicker: What landed on the big services, and — more usefully — what Criterion and MUBI put up this month. The repertory shelf is the better half of the section.

blocks.text: The majors had a quiet fortnight for film: one big Netflix genre swing that doesn't quite work, and a handful of acquisitions clearing their windows. The curated services had an excellent one.

blocks.title: The Love That Remains
blocks.meta: MUBI · new to the service this month
why: The *Godland* director turns to a family working out how to live after a separation, across a full turn of the seasons in rural Iceland. Pálmason shoots landscape the way Wenders shoots road — as something that keeps happening to the people standing in it — and the film is far funnier than that description suggests.
Intimate and expansive at once, which is a hard pair to hold. If you only take one thing off MUBI this month, take this.

blocks.title: Barbara Kopple: Harlan County USA & American Dream
blocks.extraCredit: Both films won the Academy Award for Documentary Feature
why: Two of the toughest documentaries America has produced, up together. *Harlan County USA* puts Kopple's camera between striking Kentucky miners and company guns in 1973 and simply does not leave; *American Dream* follows the Hormel strike in Austin, Minnesota a decade later and watches a union come apart from the inside.

This is the American vernacular at its least sentimental — work, faith, solidarity and the exact point at which each gives way. Kopple also has a new film, *Union Town*, premiering at Toronto next month, so the timing is not an accident.

blocks.title: The Last House
blocks.desc: Louis Leterrier's sealed-house thriller with Wagner Moura and Greta Lee — strong dread, thin logic, mixed reviews.

blocks.title: Barbara Kopple: Harlan County USA, American Dream

sections.title: Festivals
sections.tocLine: Locarno on the lake; the autumn slate lands
sections.kicker: Two festivals are running as this goes out and one opens tomorrow. Meanwhile the entire autumn circuit — Venice, Telluride, Toronto, New York — showed its cards inside a fortnight.

blocks.text: This is the fortnight the year's shape becomes visible. Venice put Herzog, Kore-eda, Lee Chang-dong and McDonagh in one competition; Toronto and New York filled in around it; and Locarno is still going, with the Golden Leopard two days out.

blocks.name: Locarno 79
body: 233 films, 103 world premieres, and a seventeen-title Concorso Internazionale judged by Fabrice Du Welz. Hong Sangsoo's *Nowhere to Lay My Eyes* world-premiered today — Cinema Guild has already taken US rights — and Denis Côté's *Nobody's Violence*, about a travelling girl selling euthanasia in a dystopia, played on the 8th. Albert Serra has a new film out of competition.

Also in competition: Matheus Farias and Enock Carvalho's *A Margem do Rio*, Salvatore Mereu's *Alberi Erranti* and Maria Bäck's *Brave New Love*. Honorary awards go to Darren Aronofsky, Virginie Efira and Asia Argento; the Piazza Grande has Petra Volpe's *Frank & Louis* plus Swiss premieres for James Gray's *Paper Tiger* and Olivia Wilde's *The Invite*.
The Golden Leopard is announced when the festival closes on August 15 — it will be in next week's issue.

blocks.name: Melbourne International 74
blocks.when: August 6–23 · Melbourne, plus MIFF Online from Aug 14
body: Opened with the Australian premiere of *Wicker*, the Sundance fable from Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, with Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Peter Dinklage, Richard E. Grant and Elizabeth Debicki. It also plays in the Bright Horizons competition, with both directors in attendance.

blocks.name: Sarajevo 32
body: Opens with Paweł Pawlikowski's *Fatherland*, fresh from competition at Cannes. 51 films chase the Heart of Sarajevo across four competitions — 21 of them world premieres — chosen from 1,215 submissions. The documentary competition alone runs 22 titles out of 305 entries, nine of them world premieres.
Emily Watson chairs the feature jury. Asghar Farhadi collects the Honorary Heart of Sarajevo.

blocks.name: Fantasia 30
body: The thirtieth edition closed out with a genuinely strong slate of winners, and a French film taking the animation prize for the first time in the festival's history.
blocks.winners: *Cheval Noir, Best Film:* Nightborn (Hanna Bergholm). *Best Director:* Kasper Kalle, No Rest for the Wicked. *Acting:* Seidi Haarla; Pilou Asbæk. *Cinematography & Score:* Ferine (Andrea Corsini) — Fabrizio La Palombara, and Pino Donaggio. *Satoshi Kon Award:* Blaise (Jean-Paul Guigue, Dimitri Planchon). *Northern Excellence:* Black Zombie (Maya Annik Bedward). *Audience, International:* I Love Paris (Nicky Murphy).

blocks.name: Venice 83
body: The stacked one. Danny Boyle's *Ink* opens, Giovanni Veronesi's *Dio ride* closes, and the competition carries Werner Herzog's *Bucking Fastard* — the true story of inseparable twin sisters, played by Rooney and Kate Mara — alongside Hirokazu Kore-eda's live-action *Look Back*, Lee Chang-dong's *Possible Love*, Martin McDonagh's *Wild Horse Nine* and Florian Zeller's *Bunker*.
Maggie Gyllenhaal presides over the jury. George Clooney and Ellen Burstyn take Golden Lions for lifetime achievement.

blocks.name: Telluride 53
body: Rebecca Hall is this year's Guest Director, shaping a slice of the programme. As ever, the lineup stays sealed until the day before it opens.

blocks.name: Toronto 51
body: 293 films. Ryûsuke Hamaguchi opens the festival with *All of a Sudden*. The TIFF Docs slate landed on August 5 — 21 titles from 20 countries, 18 of them world premieres, more than two-thirds directed by women. Rebeca Huntt's *Rapinoe* opens the section; Alex Gibney brings *Musk*; Barbara Kopple brings *Union Town*, on the current New York labour fights.
The final additions include Peter Ho-Sun Chan's *The Road Not Taken*, Cody Fern's *Closing Night*, and McDonagh's *Wild Horse Nine* moving north from the Lido.

blocks.name: New York 64
blocks.when: September 25 – October 12 · Film at Lincoln Center
body: 32 films from 31 countries in the Main Slate, announced this month. James Gray's *Paper Tiger* opens as a North American premiere; Tony Gilroy's *Behemoth!* is the centrepiece; Ava DuVernay's documentary *14th* closes. Cannes winners *Minotaur*, *Fatherland* and *All of a Sudden* all make the cut, and seventeen directors are in the Main Slate for the first time.

blocks.name: Sundance 2027
body: Dates and venues confirmed for the first Boulder edition after the long Park City run. World premieres run January 21–26, at-home screenings January 28–31, awards on the 29th. Programming will not be announced until much closer to the festival; volunteer applications open August 31.

wildcard.kicker: One film a week that isn't new, chosen off the same instincts as the picks.
wildcard.title: God's Angry Man
wildcard.extraCredit: West German television, as *Glaube und Währung*
body: Herzog spends three-quarters of an hour with Dr. Gene Scott — Stanford PhD, ordained minister, Los Angeles broadcaster — as he sits in a studio at three in the morning refusing to preach until the phones ring with enough money. He waits. He glares into the lens. He berates his own congregation. Then he waits some more, and Herzog just keeps rolling.

It is the missing link between everything else on your list. The belief systems of *Wild Wild Country*, the American vernacular strangeness that *How To with John Wilson* wanders into, the deadpan portraiture Errol Morris was building at exactly the same moment in *Vernon, Florida* — all of it is here, in a film short enough to watch before dinner. Herzog is not mocking Scott and he is not defending him. He is doing the harder thing, which is watching a man construct a reality on television and letting the camera hold long past the point of comfort.

The FCC was trying to shut Scott down throughout. That fight is the film's engine, but its real subject is the silence between the pleas — a broadcaster alone in a room, waiting for proof that anyone is out there.
wildcard.where: Tubi (free), Prime Video, and the Internet Archive
